title: The shape of a week
hookLine: worship, rest, friends, fast, feast, give
tomorrow: which month won't leave any room unless you plan it early?

cards: A calendar app shows a week as a grid: meetings, errands, a dentist appointment, a pickup. Nothing on the grid says what the week is for. Take a pen instead and draw seven boxes by hand.
The pen drags a little on the paper; the lines come out crooked. Then, one by one, the boxes fill with the practices of these past days, and something shows up that no single box could show: a shape.

teach.b: Ecclesiastes has the line for it, in the King James Bible: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.” Here are the purposes.
Worship, where the line was gather: people around word and table. A sabbath: rest is holy, made for people. A small group: two or three.
A fast day: small, quiet, safe. A shared meal: break bread, and leave a chair for someone. A letter: encourage, by naming what you've seen.
A creation walk: consider the lilies. A generous act, planned in the heart. And the weekly check: first be reconciled.
Now look at the page, because pairs are hiding on it.
A fast and a feast. Quiet and company. Receiving rest and giving gifts.
Looking up at the sky and looking across at a person. Saying sorry and saying thank you. The shape isn't a checklist to pass.
If a box goes empty, the week isn't ruined; you start again at the next one, the way the day's rhythm worked.
That's why the line says grace: a gift, not a grade.
And something to tell a friend tonight: every one of those boxes came from a text, not an app.

how: Some Christians keep a written rule of life, a simple weekly plan that sets times for worship, rest, prayer with others, fasting, shared meals and giving, and revisit it when life changes.

games.q: what does “the shape of a week” mean?
o: a strict schedule that leaves no time unplanned
a weekly rhythm of worship, rest, friends and giving
the order of readings for each Sunday of the year

games.q: the pieces of the week — tap the pairs.

s: a week of grace is a checklist you pass or fail
if a box goes empty, you start again at the next one. grace is a gift, not a grade.
this week's practices hold both a fast and a feast
a fast day and a shared meal sit side by side in the same week.
Ecclesiastes says there's a time to every purpose
to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.

games.q: your friend color-coded a perfect weekly plan, missed two boxes by Tuesday, and wants to scrap the whole thing. what does the shape of a week say?
o: keep the shape; start again at the next box.
scrap it; a plan you can't keep is worthless.
make it stricter, so she can't miss again.
games.why: the shape isn't a checklist. if a box goes empty, start again at the next one: a gift, not a grade.

practice: With a pen, draw seven boxes on a page and put one of these practices in each, wherever it fits your real week. Leave a box empty if nothing fits yet, and put a small mark where a fast sits next to a feast.
Go slowly, and listen to the scratch of the pen as the shape comes in.

wordCard.voice: The shape of a week. Worship, rest, friends, fast, feast and giving, drawn on one page, held loosely, and kept by grace.

orig.note: Greek for grace, a gift freely given, from the New Testament.

carryVoice: Your line: a week of grace. Crooked boxes count; the shape is the gift. Day 1705, drawn.
